sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: State True or False: (i) Supervision is very essential for indoor play activities. (ii) Play activities that involve running, jumping and walking help in large muscle coordination.
questions.answer: (i) False — the lesson says supervision is very essential for outdoor play activities (indoor play also needs adults nearby). (ii) True.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Arranging objects according to their height is an activity of the ________ domain. (ii) Activities promoting fine and gross motor skills belong to the ________ domain.
questions.answer: (i) cognitive (ii) psychomotor

questions.q: Answer briefly: (i) What characterises parallel play in children? (ii) At what stage of play do children begin to cooperate and focus on achieving group goals?
questions.answer: (i) Children play side by side, often with similar toys and mimicking each other, but not with each other. (ii) Cooperative play.

questions.q: Answer in one word or phrase: (i) Write an activity for cognitive development. (ii) Write an activity for language development.
questions.answer: (i) For example, puzzles, sorting objects by colour or size, memory games, picture completion. (ii) For example, storytelling, puppet play, picture conversation, rhymes.
questions.note: April 2024 also asked for an activity for the affective domain (e.g. dramatising stories).

questions.q: Match: (a) Practice play (b) Symbolic play — (i) Representational system develops (ii) Major role of senses during play (iii) Children use imagination

Fill in the blanks: (i) 5–12-year-old children understand rules and prefer games like football and ________. (ii) The theme for play activities must be planned according to the ________ and interest of children.
questions.answer: (i) basketball (any game with rules) (ii) age

questions.q: State True or False: (i) A six-month-old infant in a pram watching children on a slide is enjoying onlooker play. (ii) Arrangement of play materials has no influence on children's activities.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) False.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Describe and differentiate dramatic play and games with rules given by Smilansky.
questions.answer: Dramatic play: children use imagination to turn objects into something else and act out roles (shopkeeper, mother). Games with rules: competitive games in which children understand, accept and play by rules. Dramatic play is free and imaginative; games with rules are structured and come later.

questions.q: Describe onlooker play with an example.
questions.answer: In onlooker play a child watches others play but does not join; the child may talk to them to learn about the game. It is common at about 2½–3½ years. Example: a child stands near children playing with blocks, watching and asking questions, without building.

questions.q: Describe any two levels of play given by Piaget.
questions.answer: Any two: practice play (0–2 years, sensorimotor — repeated body movements, putting objects in the mouth, blowing spit bubbles); symbolic play (2–7 years — an object stands for something, make-believe and role play); games with rules (7–11 years — accepting rules, structured social play).

questions.q: Discuss the physical and social values of play.
questions.answer: Physical: activates different parts of the body, uses surplus energy that would otherwise make children irritable, and coordinates muscles and purposeful movement. Social: children form friendships, learn cooperation, social manners and ways of solving problems with friends through maximum social contact.

questions.q: Discuss the therapeutic and recreational values of play.
questions.answer: Therapeutic: play releases pent-up emotions — shy children enjoy being with others, aggressive ones learn to wait for their turn, over-competitive ones learn to accept loss, insecure ones gain self-respect. Recreational: play gives enjoyment and relaxation, keeps children emotionally satisfied and prevents boredom.

questions.q: What is symbolic play?
questions.answer: Play in which a child uses an object as a symbol of something else — for example, a wooden block as a telephone — and engages in make-believe and role play; Piaget placed it at 2–7 years.
questions.note: April 2022 asked for a one-sentence explanation.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: How does play develop?
questions.answer: Play changes with biological, social, emotional and intellectual maturity. First two years: sensorimotor play with body movements, object play from 4–5 months, symbolic play after the first year, social play with adults from about 1½ years. Two to five: play becomes purposeful; groups grow and playmates are chosen by age and gender; solitary and parallel play; make-believe and dramatic play (shopkeeper, family). Five to twelve: play becomes systematic, logical and rule-dominated, with competitive games like football and basketball.

questions.q: What factors should be considered in designing an environment conducive to play and early learning?
questions.answer: Ease of supervision and guidance; attention to safety; maximum space for free movement; children's interests; needs of the group and of each child; special activities placed where they are readily available; similar activities kept together; furniture and shelves of suitable size and height. Materials should be attractive and within children's reach, and adults should be present to interact.

questions.q: Describe planning a play activity on the theme 'water'.
questions.answer: Plan for a week in line with children's age and interest. Cognitive: talk about uses and sources of water, sort things that float and sink, measure and pour water into containers of different sizes. Language: rhymes and stories about rain and rivers, picture talk. Creative: paint with water colours, make paper boats. Physical: water play in tubs, pouring and squeezing sponges. Social and health: discuss saving water and washing hands, take a walk to see a pond or tap.

questions.q: What is meant by a thematic approach in planning play activities?
questions.answer: Play activities in all domains are planned around a theme from the children's environment — such as myself, family, food, water, clothes, seasons, people who help me — for a week or two. The theme suits the children's age and interest, builds on first-hand, concrete experiences and broadens ideas they are familiar with, instead of imposing knowledge subject by subject.
questions.note: April 2022 asked: what is a theme-based ECCE programme? Discuss with an example.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: Explain the types of play in early years with examples.
questions.answer: Piaget: practice play (0–2, repeated movements, mouthing objects), symbolic play (2–7, block as a telephone, role play), games with rules (7–11, structured games). Smilansky: functional play (playing with objects, physical movement), constructive play (building towers with blocks), dramatic play (imaginative role play), games with rules (competitive games). Parten (social): unoccupied play (newborns, not engaged), solitary play (alone with different toys), onlooker play (watching others), parallel play (side by side with similar toys), associative play (3–4 years, together without common goals), cooperative play (organised groups with roles and group goals, e.g. a team game).

or.q: Describe any two activities for social development among children.
or.answer: (1) Group games and play — e.g. passing the ball in a circle or a relay: children take turns, follow rules, cooperate and learn to accept losing. (2) Group celebrations — e.g. celebrating each child's birthday or a festival together: children share, help in arranging things, appreciate others and feel part of a group. Also cleaning the work place together and dramatising stories.

questions.q: Explain the term 'play'. Suggest the steps you would take to identify equipment and materials for outdoor play for children of 4–6 years.
questions.answer: Play is a child's freely chosen, joyful, creative activity of mind and body without externally imposed goals; Montessori called it the work of the child. Steps: (1) observe the children's interests, abilities and needs, including those with disabilities; (2) list equipment for large-muscle activities — running, climbing, jumping, sliding, swinging, balancing: balance beams, slides, swings, merry-go-round, jungle gym, materials for group games (ball, bat), water play, sand pit, tricycles; (3) check safety, sturdiness, size and height, and enough pieces for the group; (4) plan the space — paths for tricycles, sand and water areas, fixed swings and slides, open green space — so supervision is easy; (5) prefer low-cost and local materials such as old tyres; (6) rearrange with the seasons and review use.

or.q: Describe play activities in the context of children. Discuss the role of the teacher in promoting children's play in a centre.
or.answer: Play activities cover all domains: cognitive and language (puzzles, sorting, stories, role play), affective (dramatisation, songs, dressing dolls), psychomotor (throwing, jumping, threading beads, clay). Teacher's role: observer — watches how children interact and use materials, to plan better play; facilitator — arranges equipment and climate, lets children speak freely and encourages questions; reviewer — checks after each activity whether it met each child's needs and the curriculum goals, and informs parents; organiser — prepares a safe, happy, interesting and challenging indoor and outdoor play environment with suitable materials.
